asks.label: Tesla's battery cells
asks.question: What does Tesla disclose about its dependence on battery cell suppliers?

result.summary: Tesla relies on a very limited number of qualified lithium-ion cell suppliers, such as Panasonic and CATL, and has little flexibility to switch, so any supply disruption could limit vehicle and energy storage production. It plans to supplement supplier cells with its own, which needs significant investment and may not succeed. Cell cost and availability also depend on volatile prices of lithium, nickel and other metals.

raw_claims.quote: Currently, we rely on suppliers such as Panasonic and Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL) for these cells. We have to date fully qualified only a very limited number of such suppliers and have limited flexibility in changing suppliers.

If we are unable to do so, we may have to curtail our planned vehicle and energy storage product production or procure additional cells from suppliers at potentially greater costs, either of which may harm our business and operating results.

the cost and mass production of battery cells, whether manufactured by our suppliers or by us, depends in part upon the prices and availability of raw materials such as lithium, nickel and/or other metals.
Our plan to grow the volume and profitability of our vehicles and energy storage products depends on significant lithium-ion battery cell production.

(3) reduce the costs associated with the manufacture of EVs, particularly with respect to battery cells and packs; (4) increase vehicle range and the rate of charge and energy density of our batteries; (5) efficiently source sufficient materials for the manufacture of battery cells

asks.label: GM and Ford: the EV shift
asks.question: How are GM and Ford exposed to the transition to electric vehicles?

result.summary: Both GM and Ford face EV-transition risk through emissions and fuel-economy regulation, uncertain consumer acceptance, and dependence on charging infrastructure and battery supply. Ford also flags margin risk from mix shifts away from profitable ICE trucks and price competition in EVs, while GM highlights limits on profitably producing EVs and possible emissions credit purchases or penalties.

raw_claims.quote: such regulations could require us to further limit emissions associated with customer use of products we sell, change our manufacturing processes or product portfolio, or undertake other activities that may require us to incur additional expense, including the purchase of emissions credits or the payment of penalties

government regulations aimed at reducing emissions and increasing fuel efficiency (e.g., ZEV mandates and low emission zones) and other factors that accelerate the transition to EVs in various markets may increase the cost of vehicles by more than the perceived benefit to consumers and dampen margins.

There is no assurance that we will be able to produce and sell vehicles that use such new technologies on a profitable basis or that our customers will purchase such vehicles in the quantities necessary for us to comply with current or future regulatory requirements.

if demand for electrified vehicles grows at a rate greater than our plan or ability to increase our production capacity for those vehicles, lower market share and revenue, as well as facility and other asset-related charges (e.g., accelerated depreciation) associated with the production of internal combustion vehicles, may result.

the widespread availability (or lack thereof) of supporting infrastructure for new technologies, especially with respect to EVs, the availability (or lack thereof) of the raw materials and component supply to make batteries and other elements of EVs
the widespread availability (or lack thereof) of supporting infrastructure for new technologies, including charging for electrified vehicles

changes in industrial policy, including incentives for electrified vehicles and battery manufacturing and requirements for battery supply chains; changes in trade policy, which may affect the profitability of certain products

Ford may face increased price competition for its products and services, including pricing pressure resulting from industry excess capacity, currency fluctuations, competitive actions, legal and policy changes, or economic or other factors, particularly for electrified vehicles.
